artifacts.notes: Keyed text, not OCR. guidance/catena.md recorded that the unencumbered Latin is OCR wreckage and the clean Latin encumbered, measuring Migne PL 34's Internet Archive text layer at roughly one corrupted word in eight; that is true of the scan and false of the volume. This is the University of Zurich's Corpus Corporum encoding of Migne PL 14, keyed rather than scanned, republished on Latin Wikisource under a stated CC BY-SA 4.0 markup licence over a public-domain printing. It is a transcription of a web witness of that printing and not a collation against the printed column, so no passage taken from it rises above inspected.
artifacts.rights_basis: Ambrose of Milan's Latin as printed by Migne in 1845, in the public domain by age of both the text and the printing. No host's markup, navigation, headings, categories or column apparatus is reproduced, and the Corpus Corporum encoding note has been removed, so nothing of the contributors' or the encoder's own work survives in these bytes.

artifacts.notes: The work occupies six wiki pages, one to a book, and the current revision of each at retrieval was 267618, 225563, 225564, 225567, 225572 and 225570 for books I to VI in order. The pages carry the Corpus Corporum encoding note recording that the file was encoded in TEI XML for the University of Zurich's Corpus Corporum project from Migne's Patrologia Latina tomus 14; that is the encoder's statement about the file and is not part of Migne, and the transformation removes it.
artifacts.rights_basis: Ambrose of Milan's Latin is of the fourth century and Migne's printing is of 1845, so the text beneath these bytes is in the public domain everywhere. The bytes themselves are the wiki source of a Latin Wikisource transcription, and Latin Wikisource contributions are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 — a condition on the contributors' markup rather than on Migne's text under it. The exact bytes are therefore hashed and recorded but not retained here, and only the printed Latin reaches the tracked derivative, stripped of every template, link, heading and column marker the contributors and the encoder added.

work.author: Ambrose of Milan
work.description: Ambrose's exposition of the six days, preached in Lent and published in six books, one to a day. It follows Basil's Hexaemeron closely enough that Bede's preface names the two together, and departs from it constantly in the natural history and in the moral application Ambrose draws from every creature. It reaches the sixth day and the making of man and stops: nothing in it expounds Genesis 2 or 3 beyond the closing chapter on how God is said to have rested.
work.title: Hexameron
